profile.summary: Acts is the link between the Gospels and the rest of the New Testament: it shows how the message of Jesus came out of Jerusalem and advanced to the Mediterranean world, involving Jews and Gentiles in the same promise of salvation. The book highlights the performance of the Holy Spirit, the centrality of prayer and the testimony of key figures such as Peter and Paul. It also presents the expansion of the gospel in the midst of the opposition, showing that nothing can prevent the advancement of the word of God.
profile.setting: The action takes place in the early church period, when the good news about Jesus spread from Jerusalem throughout the region of Palestine, Syria and then the Gentile world within the Roman Empire. The context includes Jewish, Samaritan, Gentile and urban centers of the Mediterranean, culminating in Rome. The exact date and place of composition are uncertain: Rome is likely, and the date is debated between the early 60s and after 70 A.D.; many defend a previous date because the book does not mention subsequent decisive facts linked to the fall of Jerusalem or the death of apostolic leaders.

structure.label: Jerusalem and the beginning of the testimony
structure.description: The community is born and strengthened in Jerusalem, with the empowerment of the Spirit and the initial testimony of the apostles.

structure.label: Expansion for Judea, Samaria and beyond
structure.description: The message goes beyond the Jewish center and reaches new groups, showing the progressive opening of the gospel.

structure.label: First major gencyl expansion
structure.description: The mission advances to the Gentile world, with emphasis on Paul's ministry in his travels.

structure.label: Conflicts, the defense of faith and arrival in Rome
structure.description: The opposition grows, but the gospel continues to advance to Paul's testimony in Rome, where the book ends with the word still free.

themes: Salvation in Christ is for all peoples
The Holy Spirit empowers the mission of the church
Peter and Paul as central witnesses of God's plan
readingKeys: Notice how the book organizes the expansion of the message in geographical stages, from Jerusalem to Rome.
Realize public discourses as key moments to understand the theological sense of events.
Notice how prayer, Holy Spirit and witness go together and support the mission of the church.
profile.cautions: The Lucana authorship is traditional and well supported by the unity with the Gospel of Luke, but it must be treated cautiously because the introduction works with historical inferences, not with absolute proof. The date is also discussed: there are good arguments for a composition before 64 AD, but some scholars prefer after 70 AD. The introductory text privileges Luke's historical reliability and the theological purpose of the book, without requiring a closed chronology for all events.

dossier.narratedEra: The book of Acts narrates the initial apostolic phase after the ascension of Jesus, with the expansion of the church from Jerusalem to Samaria, Syria, the Greek world and, finally, Rome. The historical setting explained by the notes is that of the Roman Empire and its known rulers, with strong interaction between Jewish and Roman authorities (especially in Jerusalem, Antioch, Caesarea, Corinth, Malta and Rome).
dossier.compositionEra: The notes attribute the composition to Luke, Paul's traveling companion and author of the Gospel of Luke, writing a second work for Theophilus. As for the date, the sources record debate: many place Acts after 70 AD, but also claim that a plausible case favors composition before 64 AD, possibly in Rome, with the book ending while Paul was still under house arrest (c. 60-62 A.D.).

politics.title: Roman Empire as a frame of mission
politics.detail: The notes treat Rome and its administrative circuits as the background of the expansion of the gospel: Paul's route reaches the center of the empire, and Acts closes with him preaching in Rome in custody. The book also highlights that Christianity did not pose danger to the Roman state and could deserve protection similar to that accorded to Judaism.
politics.readingImpact: Reading Acts like this shows that the mission is neither marginal nor clandestine: it crosses imperial structures without being defined by them, and the end in Rome reinforces the universality of the message.

politics.title: Roman governors and the public defense of Paul
politics.detail: The notes quote Felix, Festus and the episode of Galio. Tyndale notes that the title given to Theophilus is also used for Roman governors, and the book's chronology is tied to the exchange of Felix Festus and Galio's proconsulate in Acaia.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read Paul's defense speeches as historical pieces located before real authorities, not as theological abstractions outside of civil power.

politics.title: Local Kingdoms under Rome: Herod Agrippa I and Judea
politics.detail: The introduction relates the death of Herod Agrippa I in 44 AD to the episode of Acts 12, indicating that Peter's persecution and incarceration occurred before that date. The source also places this within the period of the indirect Roman government in Judea.
politics.readingImpact: The reader realizes that opposition to the church comes not only from religious authorities; there is also local political power operating within the imperial structure.

politics.title: Jewish internal disputes and pressure in Jerusalem
politics.detail: Matthew Henry emphasizes that Acts show the emergence of the church - among the Jews and Samaritans" and then among the Gentiles, with strong opposition and a historical turn of the old to the new people of God. Tyndale also notes the debate on the inclusion of Gentiles in Acts 15.
politics.readingImpact: Reading gains historical tension: Christian expansion is not only geographical, but also a dispute over belonging to the people of God.

customs.title: Community prayer before action
customs.detail: The notes highlight that the first disciples in Jerusalem waited for the promised gift in prayer, with unity, worship and dependence on God. In Acts 1, until the choice of Matthias is made in prayer and by lot, a method seen as established in the Old Testament.
customs.readingImpact: This shows that the early church does not begin its mission with autonomous strategy, but with liturgical waiting and pursuit of the divine will.

customs.title: Breaking bread, meetings and community life
customs.detail: Matthew Henry describes the church as a body that meets in religious assemblies, perseveres in the doctrine of the apostles, in prayer and in the breaking of bread. This description is treated as the standard of ecclesial life that is born in Acts.
customs.readingImpact: The reading of the book ceases to be only narrating events and begins to show the emergence of concrete community habits that define the Christian identity.

customs.title: Sponsorship, social status and text circulation
customs.detail: Tyndale suggests that Theophilus was probably a benefactor/sponsor of high social status, possibly financing publication or distribution. The source notes that the title "excecellar" suggests high position.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to understand Acts as a work aimed at a concrete social network, not only anonymous readers; the dissemination of the text also depended on material means.

customs.title: Hospitality, supply and material relief
customs.detail: In Malta, the inhabitants provide the necessary to the crew, and in Antioch the church sends help to Judea during famine. The chronology section links this collection to the reign of Claudius and the period of scarcity in Judea.
customs.readingImpact: Acts show that mission and material care go together: faith is expressed in hospitality, help and concrete support.

customs.title: The itinerant life of work and travel
customs.detail: The notes emphasize real commuting: travel through commercial routes in Iconon, displacement by Licaonia, sea crossings, stop in Puteoli and the driving of Paul to Rome. In 28:16, Paul lives in his own lodge under the custody of a soldier.
customs.readingImpact: The context shows that the mission develops in ordinary conditions of travel, commerce, lodging and custody, which gives historical concreteness to the reports.

language.title: Programmatic geographical structure of Acts 1:8
language.detail: Tyndale sees 1:8 as a key verse that organizes the book in geographical expansion: Jerusalem and Judea, Samaria, Antioch and the Mediterranean world to Rome. The same note associates the closure with the Greek adverb ak-lut's (without impediment).
language.readingImpact: The reading of the book follows a theological and narrative map: the mission progresses in stages, and the open end underlines the continuity of expansion.

language.title: "Without impediment" as a key to the outcome
language.detail: The note about 28:31 states that the last Greek word highlights that the word of God cannot be imprisoned, even when its messengers are imprisoned.
language.readingImpact: The end is not defeat, but narrative triumph: Paul's custody is contrasted with the freedom of the message.

language.title: Speeches adapted to different audiences
language.detail: The introduction notes that the discourses of Peter, Stephen and Paul adjust to the cultural contexts: the sermon of Pentecost has a strongly Jewish character, while speech in Athens uses forms of Greek oratory.
language.readingImpact: This guides the reading to recognize real rhetorical variety in the book; Luke does not repeat a single style, but portrays the proclamation according to the auditorium.

language.title: First Jews, then Gentiles" as a verbal pattern
language.detail: The notes on 28:17-28 insist that the gospel was first presented to the Jews, and then to the Gentiles. In 28:28, this is formulated as a change of focus after Jewish refusal in that scenario.
language.readingImpact: This pattern shapes the missionary reading of Acts: the text does not erase Israel, but narrates the opening of the announcement to nations without separating it from its biblical roots.

language.title: Inclusion of the Gentiles and the language of "without partiality"
language.detail: The introduction underlines that Peter declares that God does not make sense of people and that the church concludes that Gentiles are fully included in the promises. This appears as Luke's central theological emphasis.
language.readingImpact: The language of inclusion corrects exclusivist readings of the book: universality is not an accessory, but narrative and doctrinal theme.

language.title: Images of courageousness, testimony and "open door."
language.detail: Matthew Henry describes the apostles as witnesses, fishers of men, light of the world and how that growing mustard-, is the growing mustard. Tyndale also uses the idea that God "opens the door of faith to the Gentiles."
language.readingImpact: These images guide Atos' reading as a work of growth, testimony and providential advancement, not only of succession of episodes.

timeline.title: Ascension and waiting in Jerusalem
timeline.detail: The ascension of Jesus occurs on the Mount of Olives; then the disciples return to Jerusalem, wait for the Spirit and replace Judas with Matthias. Tyndale's note places the ascension as the last physical appearance of Jesus.
timeline.readingImpact: This beginning frames the mission as a continuation of Christ's exaltation and as a transition between physical presence and action of the Spirit.

timeline.title: Pentecost and first public expansion
timeline.detail: The sources use Pentecost as a landmark of the beginning of missionary activity on a large scale, with the disciples full of the Spirit and the testimony first turned to the Jews.
timeline.readingImpact: Acts begins with spiritual power and public discourse, not with slow institutionalization; the chronology is shaped by immediate divine action.

timeline.title: The famine under Claudius and the aid of Antioch
timeline.detail: The famine prophesied by Agabo occurs during the reign of Claudius; the notes link this period to the journey of Barnabas and Paul brought help to Jerusalem. The chronology is associated with the range of 46-48 AD by Josephus.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone shows that Acts crosses broad social events of the empire, and that solidarity between churches is part of missionary history.

timeline.title: Galio in Corinth and the Pauline chronology
timeline.detail: Delphi's inscription is used to date the government of Galio in 51-52 AD, which helps to place Paul's stay in Corinth for eighteen months and his departure shortly after.
timeline.readingImpact: The pauline narrative ceases to be generic and is synchronized with a firm point in Roman history, reinforcing the chronological reliability of the account.

timeline.title: Prison of Paul, Feast and the change of governors
timeline.detail: The notes place Paul's prison about 57 AD, the Passover at Philippi in the spring of 57, the arrival of Festus in the summer of 59 and the trip to Rome at the end of 59/beginning of 60. The text ends with Paul's house arrest in Rome for two years.
timeline.readingImpact: This shapes the reading of the end of Acts as a progressive historical process, in which the mission advances despite custody and judicial appeal.

timeline.title: Death of James and the fall of Jerusalem as debated horizons
timeline.detail: The introduction mentions the death of James, the Lord's brother, in 62 AD, and the collapse of Jerusalem in 70 AD as important milestones that Acts do not mention. The source uses this to argue both in favor of the previous date and to recognize that others place the composition after 70 AD.
timeline.readingImpact: For reading, this means that Acts' silence on these events is part of the dating debate, not a simple isolated proof.

investigation: The sources are mostly introductory and devotional, with some punctual historical data; therefore the dossier privileges what they explicitly affirm and avoid external inferences.

There is real divergence on the date of composition: the introduction allows a post-70 AD. date, but also defends a plausible pre-64 AD case; the dossier records this as debate, without deciding beyond what the source gives.

The traditional authorship of Lucas is strongly affirmed, including the use of the first-person excerpts (thees) and the association with Colossians and Philemon; however, the source also presents him as probable Gentile and Hellenistic historian, which is an interpretative characterization of the introduction itself.

The customs described are selective: prayer, starting from bread, hospitality, material help, travel and custody appear clearly; other aspects of everyday life in Acts are not covered by the notes provided.

The language highlighted is that the notes comment in fact: 1:8, ak-lut's, adapted discourses, growth images and the formula "first to the Jews," then the Gentiles; no etymologies or analyses were not included in the sources.

The chronology presented depends on Roman and Jewish correlates mentioned by the notes themselves (Claudius, Galio, Festus, Nero, Josephus, Delphin's inscription); exact dates remain approximate and, in some cases, debated.
dossier.limits: This dossier is deliberately selective and depends only on Tyndale and Matthew Henry's introductions and notes provided here. No external data or complementary historical knowledge were used. Therefore, several important topics of Acts are left untreated: not all rulers, cities, social practices or literary resources of the book appear in the attached notes. There are also controversies that the sources mention without solving, especially the date of Athos' composition and the use of silence about certain events as a chronological argument. Where the source offered confessional or inferential reading, this was maintained as an interpretation, not as independent historical proof.
